legend.prereqs: Flat token list: course refs {subject, number, minGrade} joined by 'And'/'Or' strings; nested arrays are parenthesized groups. minGrade is the minimum passing grade required.
legend.coreqs: Courses that must be taken in the same term.
legend.offerings.terms: Past/scheduled terms by Banner code (YYYY = academic-year END year; Fall runs in YYYY-1). sections/enrolled/capacity are snapshots from the scheduled scrape, NOT live seat availability.
legend.offerings.typicalDays: Weekdays on which at least 50% of recent sections met.
legend.offerings.daysPct: Percent of recent sections meeting on each weekday (M/T/W/Th/F).
legend.offerings.meetingPatterns: [pattern, percent-of-sections] pairs; in patterns like 'MWR', R means Thursday.
legend.instructors: Per season. sharePct = average percent of that season's enrolled students taught by this professor (recent terms). 'reviews' links their RateMyHusky page when one exists.
legend.level: undergrad for course numbers below 5000, grad otherwise.
legend.typicallyOffered: Seasons in which the course was scheduled in at least two-thirds of that season's terms on record since it first appeared — a pattern, not a guarantee.
legend.unlocks: Courses that list this course in their prerequisites — what taking it opens up.
legend.nuPath: NUpath general-education attributes this course carries.
legend.repeatable: Whether the course may be taken more than once for credit (repeatMax / repeatMaxSH cap it).

courses.subject: LPSC
courses.title: Introduction to Law
courses.description: Examines the role of law and society from a regulatory, constitutional, and judicial perspective, noting the role each of these has played in shaping the current legal framework in the United States. Introduces students to the relationship between law, societal organizations (both nongovernmental organizations and not-for-profit organizations), the private sector, and the separate branches of government (the judiciary, congressional, and executive branches). Provides students with the opportunity to learn to legally analyze judicial opinions, prepare legal memoranda, and present an oral argument before a “judge.”

courses.subject: LPSC
courses.title: Introduction to Law, Policy, and Society
courses.description: Examines the relationship of society to its laws: how society creates changes in law or policy via societal pressure and social movements (such as the environmental, women’s rights, and corporate accountability movements); how law and policy affect individual rights and behavior; whether a society needs laws in order to function; the relationship between some branches of our government in effectuating social change; and some of the fundamental differences between societies governed by seemingly similar but pragmatically different laws, such as the right to a jury trial.

courses.subject: LPSC
courses.title: Understanding the Modern Supreme Court
courses.description: Offers a historical overview of the Supreme Court’s role in American life, focusing on the 20th century. As a legal, political, and policymaking institution, the Supreme Court plays a central role in U.S. legal, political, and policy disputes. The justices possess a wide range of social, cultural, political, and economic views.

courses.subject: LPSC
courses.title: Law and Policy in the Nation's Capital
courses.description: Offers students an opportunity to travel to Washington, D.C., to meet with attorneys in the government, nonprofit, and private sectors; witness hearings; and see the various ways law and policy are made in our nation's capital. Upon return, students write a reflective paper connecting some of the readings provided in advance (democratic theory, overview of each branch of government, adversarial legalism, law of agencies) to speaker(s) and events from the visit. May be repeated twice, based on annual unique theme.

courses.subject: LPSC
courses.title: Law and the City
courses.description: Examines key legal structures, court decisions, and social research to consider the ability of cities to make and implement public policies that directly affect the everyday lives of millions of people. American cities and their residents are frequently faced with similar legal and political questions. Topics include federalism, land-use planning and development, business regulation, gun control, school choice, public health, and climate adaptation initiatives.

courses.subject: LPSC
courses.title: Strategizing Public Policy
courses.description: Provides a practical overview to crafting effective strategies for advancing public policy changes at the federal, state, and local level using a range of legislative, litigation, and other policy tools. Uses a series of case studies on a wide range of policy topics to understand and evaluate how different policy strategies evolve in the interplay between branches and levels of government. Takes an interbranch perspective on how policy is made and places particular emphasis on the role litigation and the courts play in policy making, an aspect of public policy formulation that is often downplayed or overlooked.

courses.subject: LPSC
courses.title: Cities, Sustainability, and Climate Change
courses.description: Provides an overview of the various aspects of urban sustainability planning. Examines sustainability as an urban planning approach with both ecological and social justice goals. Covers sustainable planning and offers students an opportunity to understand it within the context of smart growth and the new urbanism. Focuses on the two areas in which cities can reduce energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions—the built environment and transportation. From there, the course examines planning efforts to reduce demand on water and sewer systems and to create employment in renewable energy and other “clean-tech” occupations. The course ends by placing urban initiatives in the context of state and national policy.
